solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Channel head left light entertainment programme

parts.note: port = the left side of a ship
to light on something = to land on it
the bill = the list of acts in a show

explanation.surface: A TV channel boss has quit the light entertainment schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel head' reads as a television executive, but the Channel is the English Channel and a head is a headland. Portland Bill is the rocky tip of the Isle of Portland on the Dorset coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Portland Bill is a headland jutting into the English Channel.

clue.text: Stress having the narrowest of leads

definitions.meaning: a phrasal verb meaning to emphasise or highlight
the smallest possible margin on a scoreboard: a single scoring unit ahead

explanation.surface: Under pressure because the lead in the match is razor-thin.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the scoreboard reading: a side that is a point up leads by the smallest margin there is.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for emphasise, plus the literal scoreline of a side ahead by the minimum.

clue.text: Pound taken from account replaced by current statement

indicators.note: its place is filled by the word for current

parts.note: a relation = an account or narrative, as in the relation of events
L = pound sterling, as in the £ sign

explanation.surface: A bank statement shows a pound debited and a current account credited.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is pure banking, with 'account' and 'current' as a bank account, but current here means present-day. Swap the L in RELATION for PRESENT and RE-PRESENT-ATION appears.
explanation.definitionFit: A representation is a formal statement of a case, as in making representations to a council.

clue.text: Member I criticise for work as parliamentarian

parts.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: An MP admits to attacking a colleague's record in the chamber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' tempts as a Member of Parliament, which suits the surface, but it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: To legislate is to make laws, which is a parliamentarian's work.

clue.text: Woman with habit takes ecstasy instead of upping painkiller

indicators.note: the nun takes the other letters inside her
in a down clue, sending letters up reads them backwards

parts.note: for = instead of, as in 'substitute this for that'

explanation.surface: A nun gives up her painkillers and turns to ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instead of' looks like a swap instruction, but it only supplies a word, which 'upping' then turns round along with the ecstasy. Nurofen is a UK brand of ibuprofen.
explanation.definitionFit: Nurofen is a brand of ibuprofen sold as a painkiller.

clue.text: Broadcast by Adele held up on secure line

indicators.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it, so the letters are scattered

explanation.surface: A radio station plays an Adele song that was delayed by a faulty connection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' and Adele set up radio, and 'held up' looks like delayed, but a climber is belayed when held on a rope anchored to something fixed.
explanation.definitionFit: A belayed climber is held up by a rope made fast to a secure point.

clue.text: Kosher joint of lamb maybe just the thing

parts.note: a leg is one joint of lamb among others
'it' = exactly the thing wanted, as in 'that's it'

explanation.surface: A butcher recommends a kosher cut of lamb as ideal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kosher' reads as a food law beside the lamb, but it is used in its slang sense of genuine or above board.
explanation.definitionFit: Legit and kosher are both slang for legitimate or above board.

clue.text: Doctor who flew over a mile received guard on landing

definitions.text: Doctor who flew over a mile

parts.note: a bannister is the rail guarding a stair landing

explanation.surface: A doctor flies a long way, gets a message, and meets an escort when the plane lands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flew' and 'landing' paint an aircraft, but the doctor ran: neurologist Roger Bannister was the first to run a mile in under four minutes, in 1954.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Roger Bannister, a doctor, famously sped over a mile in under four minutes.

clue.text: Dusty tray quiet old man fills again when empty

indicators.note: an emptied word keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: AGAIN with its middle removed leaves A…N

explanation.surface: An old man silently refills a dusty tray whenever it runs out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Again when empty' reads as refilling the tray, but it strips a word to its outside letters. An ash pan is the tray under a fire grate that catches the ash.
explanation.definitionFit: An ash pan is the tray beneath a grate that collects the ash, so it is dusty by design.

clue.text: Popular gorge full of litter

parts.note: to pig = to eat greedily, to gorge

explanation.surface: A well-known ravine has become strewn with rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gorge' looks like a ravine and 'litter' like rubbish, but litter here is a brood of piglets: a sow that is in pig is pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: A sow in pig is pregnant, carrying a litter.

clue.text: Practising engineers keen to sue when titanium's not used

parts.note: litigious = eager to go to law
Ti is the chemical symbol for titanium; LITIGIOUS loses it to become LIGIOUS

explanation.surface: Working engineers are eager to take legal action unless titanium is left out of the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Practising' looks like a verb about training engineers, but it is the adjective for someone who actively follows a faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Practising describes an active follower of a faith, the everyday sense of religious.

clue.text: New self-test laboratory's closing, being responsible for infections

indicators.note: the letters are made into something new
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: A lab that sold a new home-testing kit is shutting down, and it is to blame for spreading infections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' reads as a verb, but it is a noun here: a living creature.
explanation.definitionFit: The tsetse fly is a creature that spreads sleeping sickness.

clue.text: Player I should have said sorry to's head twisted

indicators.note: the head of 'to' is its first letter
the whole string is turned round

parts.note: a PS (postscript) adds what the writer should have said

explanation.surface: A remorseful note about an actor whom the writer failed to apologise to.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a guilty confession, but it is three pieces: a postscript, a puzzled 'sorry?' and a T, read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesp, short for thespian, is an actor, a player on the stage.

clue.text: Beard on Patrick's face ginger yet dark

indicators.note: a word's face is its front, its first letter

parts.note: the awn is the bristly beard on an ear of barley or wheat

explanation.surface: Patrick's ginger beard somehow looks dark on his face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beard' is placed 'on' P and RED, so it comes after them in an across answer. The awn is a botanical beard, not a facial one.
explanation.definitionFit: The predawn hours come before sunrise, while it is still dark.

clue.text: Spooner's broken racket in this?

indicators.note: Rev. Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words

parts.note: bust = broken; it takes the D sound from the next word
din = racket, a loud noise; it takes the B sound from the word before

explanation.surface: A smashed tennis racket belongs in the rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racket' tempts as a tennis racket that has broken, which is where the bin comes in, but it is a din, a noise. A dustbin is British for a rubbish bin.
explanation.definitionFit: A broken racket would be thrown in the dustbin.

clue.text: Alarming figure conflated soccer with war

indicators.note: two words fused into one mixed mass

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters; 'with' joins the two words

explanation.surface: A worrying statistic treats football as if it were warfare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alarming figure' suggests a scary number, but the figure is a shape in a field that alarms birds.
explanation.definitionFit: A scarecrow is a figure meant to alarm crows.

clue.text: What she has put on card fades

indicators.note: in an across answer, one word placed on another follows it

parts.note: a card is a joker, a wit

explanation.surface: Whatever she writes on her greeting card soon fades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Card' looks like a greeting card, but it is old slang for an amusing person, a joker.
explanation.definitionFit: Fades and withers share the sense of losing freshness and colour, as cut flowers do.

clue.text: The reason to admit one's singular fantasy?

indicators.note: the outer word lets the others in

explanation.surface: A dreamer asks why he should admit his one peculiar fantasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' looks possessive, but it is read as 'one is', so I (one) plus 'M ('s = is) gives I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Whimsy is playful fantasy or fanciful notion.

clue.text: Federal agents infiltrating assigned section

indicators.note: the agents get inside the other word

parts.note: set = assigned, as in set homework

explanation.surface: FBI agents have infiltrated the unit they were given.
explanation.walkthrough: G-men is US slang for FBI agents, 'government men'.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: one slice of an orange can be called either word.

clue.text: Plastic can isn't made of tin

indicators.note: plastic = mouldable, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A plastic can is, naturally, not made of tin.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a true statement about containers; 'Plastic' is the instruction, not the material. Stannic comes from stannum, Latin for tin.
explanation.definitionFit: From stannum, Latin for tin: the chemists' adjective for tin compounds.

clue.text: Odd bits of timber after sinking initially keep one man alive

indicators.note: the first letter of the word
the odd-numbered letters: 1st, 3rd and 5th
the timber letters hold ONE inside

explanation.surface: Floating bits of wood keep a man alive after his ship goes down.
explanation.walkthrough: The survival story is a decoy: 'man alive' is not a rescue but an exclamation of surprise, and 'keep' puts the survivor inside the timber letters.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Stone me!' and 'man alive!' are both British exclamations of surprise.

clue.text: Blind cat has penetrated airport's controlled area

indicators.note: the cat has got inside the other word

parts.note: to blind = to swear, as in effing and blinding; to cuss
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A blind cat has slipped into the restricted zone at an airport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blind' looks like an adjective for the cat, but it is a verb: to blind is British slang for to swear, from 'effing and blinding'.
explanation.definitionFit: Customs is the controlled area where an airport checks arriving goods.

clue.text: Word during service that must be repeated back

parts.note: in = during, as in 'in the war'

indicators.note: the service word is read backwards

parts.note: in tennis a let is a serve that must be played again

explanation.surface: A word spoken during a church service has to be repeated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' suggests church, but it is a tennis serve. 'Word' here means information, as in 'send word'.
explanation.definitionFit: Word in the sense of news, as in 'send word', matches the slang for gathered information.

clue.text: Raised border mainly contains plant with colourful flowers

indicators.note: most of the word: its last letter is dropped
the border word holds the other inside

parts.note: LINE, a border, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A gardener's raised bed is mostly given over to a bright flowering plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised border' reads as a garden bed, which suits the plant, but 'raised' is UP and 'border' is LINE.
explanation.definitionFit: The lupin is a garden plant with tall spikes of colourful flowers.

clue.text: Shopping sounded more revolting every second for hikers

indicators.note: spoken, so the word's sound is used

parts.note: grosser = more revolting; GROCER is said the same way

indicators.note: take the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters

parts.note: every second letter of hIkErS; 'for' is the link

explanation.surface: Hikers find the supplies they carried grow more disgusting by the second.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every second' suggests a time scale, but it picks out alternate letters of 'hikers'.
explanation.definitionFit: Groceries are the shopping you bring home from the supermarket.

clue.text: Pressure that is in loo breaks pump, perhaps display model

indicators.note: pressure and 'that is' go inside the loo

parts.note: a pump is a kind of shoe

indicators.note: the loo splits the shoe open and sits inside

explanation.surface: Water pressure in the toilet has broken the pump, so now it is just for show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pump' looks like plumbing beside the loo, but a pump is a light dancing shoe; loo is British for toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A showpiece is a model put on display as the finest example.

clue.text: Mature Trollope somewhat like earlier works

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used

explanation.surface: Anthony Trollope's later novels resemble his early ones.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist Trollope is only there to supply letters across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: Retro means imitating the style of earlier times or works.

clue.text: Doctor drew iron shot, putting it straighter

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it

explanation.surface: A golfer's doctor pulled an iron shot while trying to hit it straight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a person and 'drew' like a golf shape, but doctor is the verb and the definition is a phrase introducing a plainer version.
explanation.definitionFit: 'In other words' introduces a restatement put more plainly.
